summary.text: Construct a two-generated group \(P\) of order \(3^6\) for which a finite enumeration of the generator images satisfying its defining relations gives \(|\operatorname{Aut}(P)|=3^7\). Then \(C_2\times P\) has order \(2\cdot3^6=1458\) but still has automorphism group of order \(3^7=2187\), since its coprime Sylow factors are characteristic and \(\operatorname{Aut}(C_2)\) is trivial, contradicting the required order \(3^6=729\) at \(n=2\).

full_proof.text:
We disprove the order assertion in the conjecture at \(n=2\). The second prime is \(p_2=3\), so
\[
a(2)=3^7=2187.
\]
The conjecture would therefore require every finite group with automorphism group of order \(2187\) to have order
\[
\frac{2187}{3}=729.
\]
We construct instead a group of order \(1458\) whose automorphism group has order \(2187\).

Throughout the construction, all coordinates and all coordinate arithmetic are in
\[
R=\mathbb Z/27\mathbb Z.
\]
For \(j,l\in R\), let \(\bar j,\bar l\in\{0,1,\ldots,26\}\) denote their standard representatives, and define
\[
F(j)=7^{\bar j}\pmod {27}
\]
and
\[
C(j,l)=
\begin{cases}
9,&\bar j+\bar l\geq 27,\\
0,&\bar j+\bar l<27.
\end{cases}
\]
The value \(C(j,l)\) records the carry when the representatives of \(j\) and \(l\) are added, with each carry assigned the value \(9\) in the first coordinate.

Define a multiplication on the set
\[
P=R\times R
\]
by
\[
(i,j)(k,l)=\bigl(i+F(j)k+C(j,l),\ j+l\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]
Its identity is \((0,0)\), and an inverse is given by
\[
(i,j)^{-1}= igl(-F(-j)i-C(-j,j),-j\bigr).
\tag{2}
\]
We briefly justify that this is a group. The elementary congruences needed for associativity are
\[
F(j+l)=F(j)F(l),
\tag{3}
\]
\[
F(j)C(l,n)=C(l,n),
\tag{4}
\]
and
\[
C(j,l)+C(j+l,n)=C(l,n)+C(j,l+n).
\tag{5}
\]
All these identities are in \(R\). For (3), changing an exponent by \(27\) does not affect the result modulo \(27\), and the usual exponent law applies. For (4), the assertion is immediate when the carry is zero; when it is \(9\), it follows from \(7^{\bar j}\equiv1\pmod3\), and hence \(9\cdot7^{\bar j}\equiv9\pmod {27}\). Identity (5) says that the total carry in adding three standard representatives is independent of whether the first two or the last two are added first. Multiplying out both \(((i,j)(k,l))(m,n)\) and \((i,j)((k,l)(m,n))\), identities (3)--(5) make their first coordinates equal, while their second coordinates are equal by associativity in \(R\). Formula (2) is checked by substitution in (1). Thus \(P\) is a group. Since its underlying set is \(R^2\),
\[
|P|=27^2=729=3^6.
\tag{6}
\]

Put
\[
a=(1,0),\qquad b=(0,1).
\]
Repeated use of (1) gives
\[
a^m=(m,0)
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(m\), and, for \(0\leq m\leq26\),
\[
b^m=(0,m).
\]
Consequently every \((i,j)\in P\) has the normal form
\[
(i,j)=a^{\bar i}b^{\bar j}.
\tag{7}
\]
In particular, \(a,b\) generate \(P\). Direct calculation gives the three relations
\[
a^{27}=1,\qquad b^{-1}ab=a^4,\qquad b^{27}=a^9.
\tag{8}
\]
Equivalently, the middle relation can be written
\[
ba=a^7b,
\tag{9}
\]
because \(4\cdot7\equiv1\pmod {27}\).

We next count the automorphisms of \(P\). Suppose \(x,y\in P\) satisfy the analogues of (8):
\[
x^{27}=1,\qquad y^{-1}xy=x^4,\qquad y^{27}=x^9.
\tag{10}
\]
Then the formula
\[
\phi_{x,y}(i,j)=x^{\bar i}y^{\bar j}
\tag{11}
\]
defines a homomorphism \(P\to P\), sending \(a\) to \(x\) and \(b\) to \(y\). Here is the multiplication check. From the middle relation in (10) and \(x^{27}=1\), one obtains
\[
yx=x^7y,
\]
and therefore, by induction,
\[
y^j x^k=x^{7^j k}y^j.
\tag{12}
\]
When the exponents of two powers of \(y\) cross \(27\), the last relation in (10) replaces \(y^{27}\) by \(x^9\); that replacement is exactly the term \(C(j,l)\) in (1). Thus (12), together with the carry term, shows that (11) respects (1).

Conversely, every endomorphism is determined by its values on the generators \(a,b\), and those values must satisfy (10). Such an endomorphism is an automorphism precisely when \(x,y\) generate \(P\). We now translate both the relations and the generation condition into coordinates.

Write
\[
x=(i_1,j_1),\qquad y=(i_2,j_2).
\]
Repeated multiplication in (1) gives the following useful power formulas:
\[
(u,v)^{27}=(9v,0),
\tag{13}
\]
and, when \(3v=0\) in \(R\),
\[
(u,v)^4=(4u+v,4v),\qquad (u,v)^9=(9u,0).
\tag{14}
\]
Using these formulas in (10), and comparing the two coordinates, one finds that (10) is equivalent to the following three congruences in \(R\):
\[
3j_1=0,
\tag{15}
\]
\[
i_1+C(j_1,j_2)=F(j_2)(4i_1+j_1)+C(j_2,4j_1),
\tag{16}
\]
and
\[
9j_2=9i_1.
\tag{17}
\]
Notice that \(i_2\) does not occur in these conditions.

For completeness, we also explain the generation criterion. Reduce both coordinates modulo \(3\), obtaining a homomorphism
\[
\pi:P\longrightarrow (\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z)^2,
\qquad
\pi(i,j)=(i\bmod3,j\bmod3).
\tag{18}
\]
It is a homomorphism because \(F(j)\equiv1\pmod3\) and every carry is divisible by \(3\). It is surjective since
\[
\pi(a)=(1,0),\qquad \pi(b)=(0,1).
\]
The kernel consists of elements whose two coordinates are divisible by \(3\). It lies in every maximal subgroup of \(P\): indeed, every maximal subgroup of the finite \(3\)-group \(P\) has index \(3\), so every cube maps trivially to the quotient; an element in \(\ker\pi\) is, by (7), a product of powers of \(a^3\) and \(b^3\), and hence belongs to every maximal subgroup. Thus \(\ker\pi\) is contained in the Frattini subgroup. It follows from the standard nongenerating property of the Frattini subgroup that elements generate \(P\) whenever their images generate \((\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z)^2\).

Under conditions (15)--(17), reduction modulo \(3\) gives
\[
j_1\equiv0\pmod3,
\qquad
j_2\equiv i_1\pmod3.
\tag{19}
\]
A direct check of (16) modulo \(27\), subject to (15) and (17), shows that
\[
i_1\equiv0\quad\hbox{or}\quad1\pmod3;
\tag{20}
\]
the residue \(2\) cannot occur. If \(i_1\equiv0\pmod3\), then (19) implies that the second coordinates of both \(x\) and \(y\) vanish modulo \(3\), so their images cannot generate the quotient in (18), and therefore \(x,y\) do not generate \(P\). If \(i_1\equiv1\pmod3\), then
\[
\pi(x)=(1,0),\qquad \pi(y)=(i_2\bmod3,1).
\]
These vectors form a basis of \((\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z)^2\), so \(x,y\) generate \(P\). We have therefore proved:

An ordered pair \((x,y)\) is the image of \((a,b)\) under an automorphism of \(P\) if and only if (15)--(17) hold and
\[
i_1\equiv1\pmod3.
\tag{21}
\]

It remains to count these pairs. We give the finite modular enumeration explicitly. Condition (15) restricts \(j_1\) to
\[
j_1\in\{0,9,18\}.
\]
Condition (21) restricts \(i_1\) to the nine values
\[
i_1\in\{1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22,25\}.
\]
For each such \(i_1\), condition (17) initially restricts \(j_2\) to the nine residues congruent to \(1\) modulo \(3\). Substitution into (16), using the definition of the carry and the powers of \(7\) modulo \(27\), leaves exactly the following possibilities:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
j_1&j_2\\ \hline
0&1,10,19\\
9&4,13,22\\
18&7,16,25.
\end{array}
\tag{22}
\]
This table is independent of which of the nine allowed values of \(i_1\) is chosen. To see directly how the finite check is organized, the powers of \(7\) modulo \(27\) have period \(9\): for exponents \(0,1,\ldots,8\) they are
\[
1,7,22,19,25,13,10,16,4,
\]
and then repeat. For each of the three possible values of \(j_1\), inserting these nine values and the two possible carry values \(0,9\) in (16) gives precisely the corresponding row of (22), with no other cases. Thus there are
\[
3\cdot9\cdot3=81
\]
admissible triples \((i_1,j_1,j_2)\). Finally, the coordinate \(i_2\) is unrestricted and has \(27\) choices. Therefore
\[
|\operatorname{Aut}(P)|=81\cdot27=2187=3^7.
\tag{23}
\]

The group \(P\) itself has order \(729\), so it would not yet contradict the conjectured order formula. We now adjoin a factor of order \(2\) without changing the automorphism group. Let
\[
G=C_2\times P.
\]
Then
\[
|G|=2\cdot729=1458.
\tag{24}
\]
We claim that every automorphism of \(G\) fixes the \(C_2\) factor and preserves the \(P\) factor, and hence
\[
\operatorname{Aut}(G)\cong\operatorname{Aut}(P).
\tag{25}
\]

Both factors can be characterized intrinsically. Since every element of \(P\) has order dividing \(|P|=729\), for \((c,p)\in C_2\times P\) we have
\[
(c,p)^{729}=(c^{729},1)=(c,1),
\]
because \(729\) is odd. Hence
\[
(c,p)^{729}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c=1.
\]
Thus \(\{1\}\times P\) is precisely the set of elements whose \(729\)-th power is the identity, so it is characteristic.

Similarly, \(P\) has no nonidentity element of order dividing \(2\), because the order of every element of \(P\) divides the odd number \(729\). Therefore
\[
(c,p)^2=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=1.
\]
Thus \(C_2\times\{1\}\) is also characteristic. Every automorphism of \(G\) consequently restricts to automorphisms of these two factors. The automorphism group of \(C_2\) is trivial, so an automorphism of \(G\) acts as the identity on \(C_2\) and as an arbitrary automorphism on \(P\). Conversely, every automorphism of \(P\), acting trivially on \(C_2\), gives an automorphism of \(G\). This proves (25). By (23),
\[
|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|=2187.
\tag{26}
\]

Finally, at \(n=2\) the relevant prime is \(p_2=3\), and since \(3\not\equiv2\pmod3\), the sequence definition uses the seventh power:
\[
a(2)=3^7=2187.
\]
Our group \(G\) therefore satisfies
\[
|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|=a(2),
\]
but
\[
|G|=1458\neq729=\frac{a(2)}{p_2}.
\]
This contradicts the asserted order formula. Hence Conjecture 2 for A365179 is false, regardless of its additional uniqueness assertion for primes congruent to \(2\pmod3\).
